title: System anatomy and access boundaries
audience: Cleaners and supervisors who need to recognise the parts of a commercial kitchen exhaust system and the limits of access.
learningOutcomes: Identify hoods, filters, ducts, fans and concealed or inaccessible sections of an exhaust system.
Separate what is observed from what is reported and what is unknown.
Refuse to sign off a system beyond the scope of the work order, and refer the question to the owner.

instruction.heading: The parts of the system
instruction.body: A commercial kitchen exhaust system usually includes a hood over the cooking line, grease filters within the hood, a duct that carries air away, a fan, and an outlet. Parts of the duct may run through walls, ceilings and roofs, so they are concealed or inaccessible from the kitchen floor. Knowing where the accessible parts end and the concealed parts begin is the first boundary in any exhaust task.

instruction.heading: Observation and assumption
instruction.body: Consider a work order that covers a hood, while a contractor proposes to sign off the whole connected system. Work through what you observe, what you are only told, and what remains unknown, and label each separately. A clean hood does not show that the duct is clean or that the fan is safe. A missing or conflicting authority is grounds to withhold action, so the sign-off is refused and the question is referred.

instruction.heading: Access and referral
instruction.body: Use the duct and access diagram to decide whether an ordinary cleaner may carry out the permitted surface task, or must stop and refer. Describe the components as you see them, without climbing, entering ductwork or operating any component. Escalate at once where ducting is inaccessible, where system ownership is unclear, or where access would need an alteration to the building or the system.

instruction.heading: Recording without certifying
instruction.body: Complete a dated record with the site zone, the authorising party, the observations, the excluded access, the evidence gaps, the referral owner and the response requested. Do not backfill permissions, and do not issue a compliance certificate. Whether the system is safe is decided by the owner and the competent person, not the cleaner.

procedure: Identify the hood, filters, ducts, fan and any concealed or inaccessible sections on the diagram.
Record what is observed, what is reported and what is unknown, separately.
Refuse any sign-off beyond the work order, and refer the question to the owner.
Do not climb, enter ductwork or operate components.
Escalate for inaccessible ducting, unclear ownership or any access that needs alteration.
Record the zone, authority, observations, exclusions and referral owner.

workedExamples.situation: A work order covers a range hood, but a contractor asks you to sign off the entire connected exhaust system.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the wider sign-off. The work order covers only the hood, and a clean hood is not evidence about the duct or the fan. Record what you observed, mark the duct as unknown, and refer the request to the system owner.

equipmentAndPpe: Duct and access diagram from the site.
Work order and the site permission record.
Gloves and eye protection for any accessible hood cleaning, as set by the SDS.

commonErrors.error: Signing off a system from a clean hood.
commonErrors.prevention: Sign off only the scope actually inspected, and refer the rest.
Label each statement as observed, reported or unknown.

commonErrors.error: Climbing into the duct to see further.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Commercial exhaust and fire-suppression systems are subject to specialist requirements and the owner's and insurer's obligations. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority, and does not certify a system.

Safety details for every chemical, hazardous or not, need to reach all people on site, and they sit on the label and the SDS. The register has to cover hazardous chemicals that are used, handled or kept on site, each entry needs an up-to-date SDS attached, and the register must be easy for workers to reach (Safe Work Australia, no date shown). Check your state or territory regulator for extra rules.

qualityStandard: Components identified on the diagram, with observed, reported and unknown kept separate.
Wider sign-off refused in the case study.
Referral recorded with the owner named.
documentationEvidence: Dated record with zone, authority, observations, exclusions and referral owner.
Refusal and referral record for any sign-off beyond scope.
summary: Know where the accessible parts end and the concealed parts begin.
Label observation, report and unknown separately.
Refuse sign-off beyond the work order and refer.

knowledgeChecks.question: A clean hood is in front of you. What does that show about the connected duct?
options: Nothing about the duct, which must be assessed by the owner
That the duct is clean all the way through to the fan
That the fan is safe to run for the next shift today

knowledgeChecks.question: A contractor asks you to sign off the whole system when the work order covers a hood. What is the correct response?
options: Sign it, to be helpful to the contractor on the day
Refuse the wider sign-off and refer it to the owner
Sign it and note that the hood only was covered in the work

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of the system should a cleaner climb or enter?
options: The hood, from a stable step on the floor
The duct, if it is accessible from the roof
None of the concealed ductwork or components

knowledgeChecks.question: How does the lesson say to treat what you observe, what you are only told, and what remains unknown?
options: Report only what the contractor says
